commit_message:
Show true error reason in `wasmtime serve` (#8026)

* Show true error reason in `wasmtime serve`

The `wasmtime serve` command prints failed HTTP handling to `stderr`
but, when the reason was due to failure inside the HTTP handler itself,
the printed error message is not descriptive enough. After looking at
long dumps of `guest never invoked `response-outparam::set` method`, I
realized that errors inside the Tokio `task` are never propagated
outwards. This change captures those errors and appends them to the
printed error message.

* review: remove TODO comment

* review: improve doc comment

Co-authored-by: Trevor Elliott <telliott@fastly.com>

* review: add comment about immediate resolution

fix_commit.message: Don’t panic when http `handle` function returns before invoking `set` (#10387)
fix_commit.author: primoly

findings.title: Reachable panic via `.expect_err()` when guest handler returns Ok without calling response-outparam::set
findings.message: In `handle_request` in `src/commands/serve.rs`, when the `receiver` oneshot channel errors out (meaning the response-outparam `set` method was never invoked by the guest), the code awaits the spawned task and calls `.expect_err("if the receiver has an error, the task must have failed")` on its result. This assumes that if the guest never called `set`, the task must have returned an `Err`. However, a guest Wasm component can legitimately return `Ok(())` from its `handle` export without ever invoking `response-outparam::set` (e.g. it simply forgets to call it, or returns early without error). In that case `task.await` yields `Ok(Ok(()))`, so `r` is `Ok(())`, and `Result::expect_err` panics because the value is not an `Err`. Since this path is driven directly by externally-supplied/untrusted Wasm guest code processing an HTTP request in the `wasmtime serve` CLI command, any malicious or buggy guest component can deterministically crash the host process serving HTTP traffic, resulting in a remotely triggerable denial of service.
findings.suggestion: Do not assume the task must have returned an error when the receiver fails. Instead, explicitly handle the `Ok(Ok(()))` case (task completed successfully but never invoked `set`) by producing a dedicated error/bail instead of calling `.expect_err()`, which panics on that input. The actual fix (commit ad21d9581d) matches on `task.await` as `Ok(Ok(())) => bail!(...)`, `Ok(Err(e)) => e`, `Err(e) => e.into()`, avoiding the panicking `expect_err` call entirely.

ground_truth.root_cause: The error-reporting logic conflated two independent failure signals: (1) the oneshot `receiver` erroring because the sender was dropped without sending a response, and (2) the task's own `Result` indicating whether an error occurred. The code assumed these always correlate (receiver error implies task error) and used a panicking `expect_err` to extract the task's error, without accounting for the case where the guest task completes with `Ok(())` yet never calls `set`.
